ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT Article history: Background: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is an Received 24 June 2025 X-linked recessive disorder that affects over 400 million people worldwide. The Accepted as revised 8 September 2025 deficit causes individuals susceptible to hemolysis during oxidative stress. In Available online 12 September 2025 newborns, G6PD deficiency can lead to hyperbilirubinemia, bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction, and kernicterus, making early detection and screening Keywords: crucial. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, rapid test, performance, Objectives: This study aimed to compare the diagnostic performance of three point-of-care, newborns. rapid screening tests for G6PD deficiency in newborns: the fluorescent spot test (FST), G6PD rapid test kit, and SD Biosensor, using spectrophotometry as the gold standard. Materials and methods: Blood samples from 70 newborns were tested using these three methods. The diagnostic performances, including sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and efficiency of each method were analyzed. Results: Both the FST and G6PD rapid test kit exhibited higher specificity, PPV, and efficiency compared to the SD Biosensor. Nonetheless, the SD Biosensor exhibited superior sensitivity and NPV, but it was unable to identify G6PD activity in 16.4% of instances due to elevated hemoglobin concentrations. Conclusion: The FST and G6PD rapid test kit are reliable and suitable for G6PD deficiency screening in newborns, especially in settings with limited resources, due to their high efficiency, specificity, and rapid results. The SD Biosensor remains a valuable tool in clinical contexts requiring high sensitivity. For newborns with high hemoglobin levels, the FST or G6PD rapid test is recommended for accurate screening. Further studies with larger sample sizes are necessary to confirm the reliability of these tests in diverse populations. JSON: Name: g6pd_newborn_screening_comparison Title: Comparative evaluation of fluorescent spot, rapid colorimetric, and biosensor point-of-care methods for newborn G6PD deficiency screening using spectrophotometry as the reference standard Short Hypothesis: In newborns, a quantitative biosensor produces higher sensitivity and negative predictive value than the fluorescent spot test and rapid colorimetric kit, but the biosensor yields a significantly higher rate of indeterminate or unanalyzable results for samples with hemoglobin >25 g/dL, reducing its effective diagnostic yield relative to the other tests. Related Work: Current diagnostic practice uses spectrophotometric enzymatic assays as the reference standard for G6PD activity quantification; however, these assays require laboratory equipment and centralized processing. The fluorescent spot test (FST) is a long-standing qualitative screening method with high reported specificity and operational simplicity but requires UV light and subjective fluorescence reading. Rapid colorimetric lateral-flow or card-based tests provide faster and simpler workflows with comparable specificity to FST in some settings but can have reduced sensitivity for intermediate activity and heterozygous females. Point-of-care biosensors deliver quantitative, hemoglobin-adjusted G6PD values suitable for decentralized testing; published device evaluations report high sensitivity and specificity in mixed-age cohorts but note device measurement ranges and hemoglobin limits that can produce indeterminate/failed analyses. Unresolved issues include: (1) performance trade-offs between qualitative rapid tests and quantitative biosensors in neonates who have higher hemoglobin and reticulocytosis; (2) device-specific Hb-range limitations and their impact on testability and false positives/negatives in newborn samples; (3) limited large-scale neonatal accuracy data and limited characterization of assay agreement and failure modes across subgroups (sex, Hb strata, reticulocyte counts). Abstract: Neonatal screening for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency must balance analytical accuracy with rapid, decentralized workflows. We propose a comparative diagnostic evaluation of three point-of-care screening modalities—fluorescent spot test (FST), a rapid colorimetric kit, and a quantitative biosensor—against spectrophotometric enzymatic assay as the gold standard in newborns. The study will measure sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, indeterminate/failure rates, quantitative agreement, and subgroup performance across hemoglobin and reticulocyte strata. The main contribution is a structured assessment of trade-offs between sensitivity and operational testability in neonates, including quantification of how elevated hemoglobin concentrations affect biosensor analyzability and effective diagnostic yield. Expected outcomes include ranked performance metrics for each method, device-specific failure profiles, and evidence to inform screening algorithms that optimize accuracy and test coverage in neonatal populations. Results will identify which point-of-care methods are most appropriate as primary screens and which require reflex testing by a reference assay in specific neonatal subgroups. Experiments: Design: Prospective, paired diagnostic accuracy study enrolling consecutive newborns at multiple birthing hospitals. Sample size: target N=800 newborns to detect a 5% absolute difference in sensitivity between methods with 80% power and alpha=0.05, with prespecified subgroup sizes (male/female, Hb bins). Inclusion: age 0–14 days, parental consent, sufficient venous or capillary blood for all tests. Exclusion: prior transfusion, major hemoglobinopathy known at birth. Index tests: (1) fluorescent spot test (FST) performed per manufacturer/ICSH protocol; (2) rapid colorimetric G6PD kit executed per kit instructions; (3) SD Biosensor quantitative G6PD device with hemoglobin-adjusted output. Reference standard: spectrophotometric G6PD enzymatic activity (NADP→NADPH absorbance at 340 nm) normalized to g Hb, performed in central lab within specified time window. Additional measurements: total hemoglobin by automated analyzer, reticulocyte percentage, and genotyping subset (n=200) for common G6PD variants. Primary endpoints: sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV) of each index test vs reference at neonatal cutoff (e.g., deficiency <3.8 U/g Hb). Secondary endpoints: device indeterminate/unanalysable rate, time-to-result, intra- and inter-operator repeatability (assessed with 20 replicate samples per device to compute coefficient of variation), quantitative agreement (Bland-Altman bias and limits-of-agreement for biosensor vs spectrophotometry), Cohen's kappa for categorical agreement, and AUC for continuous outputs where applicable. Stratified analyses: Hb bins (<20, 20–25, >25 g/dL), reticulocyte <5% vs ≥5%, sex (male hemizygotes vs female homo/heterozygotes), and genotype-positive subgroup. Statistical analysis: compute 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for sensitivity/specificity; compare paired sensitivities with McNemar's test; compare indeterminate rates with exact tests; evaluate bias with Bland-Altman and Passing–Bablok regression. Ablation studies: (A) re-evaluate accuracy excluding samples with Hb outside biosensor specs to quantify effect on effective coverage; (B) apply hemoglobin-correction algorithms or adjusted cutoffs to biosensor outputs to assess changes in false positive/negative rates; (C) simulate central-lab delay effects by re-running reference assay on stored samples at incremental timepoints to assess stability. Reporting: prespecified diagnostic statistics, confusion matrices, failure reasons, and subgroup tables. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sampling bias: enrollment at tertiary hospitals may not represent rural or ethnically diverse neonatal populations. Reference variability: spectrophotometric assays have intra-lab variability and pre-analytical susceptibility (storage time, temperature) that can confound comparisons. Device measurement limits: biosensor hemoglobin measurement or G6PD dynamic range may be exceeded in neonates, producing indeterminate results and underestimating effective sensitivity; this limitation may differ across device lots and firmware. Neonatal physiology: high neonatal hemoglobin, reticulocytosis, and recent maternal transfusion can alter assay outputs and lead to misclassification. Female heterozygotes: intermediate activity distribution complicates categorical classification and reduces apparent sensitivity/specificity for all qualitative tests. Operational variability: operator technique, UV-light interpretation (FST), and ambient conditions can introduce inter-operator and inter-site variability. Statistical constraints: subgroup sample sizes (e.g., specific genotypes) may be insufficient for precise estimates. Generalizability: results may not extrapolate to older children or adults, to devices not evaluated, or to settings with different prevalences, leading to spectrum bias. Regulatory and ethical limitations: collection of neonatal blood has volume constraints limiting repeat testing and retesting for verification.
